text: Creating an Azure virtual machine looks like one command, but it's really provisioning a small bundle of resources at once: the VM itself, an OS disk, a network interface, and usually a public IP and a network security group — all inside the resource group you point it at.

az vm create takes a resource group, a name, an image, a size, and an admin account. Here, Ubuntu2204 is the image, Standard_D2s_v5 is the size, and generate-ssh-keys creates a key pair instead of a password. Unless you say otherwise, Azure also attaches a public IP and a default network security group opening the right admin port for that OS.

Every VM size belongs to a family tuned for a specific workload. B-series is burstable: a baseline CPU level that can spend saved-up credits to burst higher for short periods, cheap for dev/test or light, spiky traffic. D-series is general purpose, a steady CPU-to-memory balance with no bursting, the default for production app servers and small databases. F-series is compute-optimized, trading memory for more raw CPU per core, built for batch jobs and analytics.

An image alias like Ubuntu2204 is shorthand for a full Marketplace URN: publisher, offer, sku, and version, such as Canonical's Ubuntu 22.04 LTS image. Aliases exist for the most common operating systems so you rarely type the full URN by hand. az vm image list shows every published image when the one you need doesn't have a shortcut alias yet.

Translate that into a decision rule: light, unpredictable traffic points to B-series; a production application server that needs steady performance all day points to D-series; a CPU-heavy batch or analytics job points to F-series. Picking the family first, then the specific size within it, keeps you from either overpaying or under-provisioning.

You now know how a VM actually gets created and how to size it sensibly. Next: what happens when the hardware underneath that VM fails — availability sets and availability zones, the two mechanisms Azure gives you to survive exactly that.
